claim: The inner nuclear membrane is functionalized by diverse transmembrane proteins that associate with nuclear lamins and/or chromatin.
source: The inner nuclear membrane is functionalized by diverse transmembrane proteins that associate with nuclear lamins and/or chromatin.
evidence: This is a general statement about INM protein function supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: When cells enter mitosis, membrane-chromatin contacts must be broken to allow for proper chromosome segregation.
source: When cells enter mitosis, membrane-chromatin contacts must be broken to allow for proper chromosome segregation
evidence: This represents established understanding in the field about mitotic requirements.

claim: An imbalance in the levels of LAP1 causes a failure in membrane removal from mitotic chromatin.
source: we observed that an imbalance in the levels of the lamina-associated polypeptide 1 (LAP1), an activator of ER-resident Torsin AAA+-ATPases, causes a failure in membrane removal from mitotic chromatin
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations described in the manuscript, including time-lapse imaging and microscopy data shown in Figure 1.

claim: LAP1 imbalance causes chromosome segregation errors.
source: an imbalance in the levels of the lamina-associated polypeptide 1 (LAP1), an activator of ER-resident Torsin AAA+-ATPases, causes a failure in membrane removal from mitotic chromatin, accompanied by chromosome segregation errors
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D quantifying segregation defects.

claim: LAP1 imbalance causes changes in post-mitotic nuclear morphology.
source: an imbalance in the levels of the lamina-associated polypeptide 1 (LAP1), an activator of ER-resident Torsin AAA+-ATPases, causes a failure in membrane removal from mitotic chromatin, accompanied by chromosome segregation errors and changes in post-mitotic nuclear morphology.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data showing nuclear envelope aberrations in Figures 1, 2, and 3.

claim: LAP1 contains a chromatin-binding region.
source: These defects are dependent on a hitherto unknown chromatin-binding region of LAP1 that we have delineated.
evidence: This is supported by mapping experiments shown in Figure 2 and EMSA data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: LAP1-induced NE abnormalities are efficiently suppressed by expression of wild-type Torsins.
source: LAP1-induced NE abnormalities are efficiently suppressed by expression of wild-type but not ATPase-deficient Torsins.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, B, and C.

claim: LAP1-induced NE abnormalities are not suppressed by expression of ATPase-deficient Torsins.
source: LAP1-induced NE abnormalities are efficiently suppressed by expression of wild-type but not ATPase-deficient Torsins.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, B, and C comparing wild-type and E178Q mutant Torsins.

claim: A dominant-negative Torsin induces chromosome segregation defects in a LAP1-dependent manner.
source: Furthermore, a dominant-negative Torsin induces chromosome segregation defects in a LAP1-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6C and D showing that LAP1 depletion reduces segregation defects caused by Tor1B(E178Q).

claim: Association of LAP1 with chromatin in the nucleus can be modulated by Torsins in the perinuclear space.
source: These results indicate that association of LAP1 with chromatin in the nucleus can be modulated by Torsins in the perinuclear space
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental results showing that Torsin activity affects LAP1 chromatin binding and mobility.

claim: Enrichment of INM proteins from the peripheral ER at the nuclear face of the NE relies on domains or motifs in their extralumenal domains that ensure retention on nuclear partners.
source: In general, enrichment of these membrane proteins from the peripheral ER at the nuclear face of the NE relies on several domains or short linear motifs in their extralumenal domains that together ensure retention on nuclear partners such as nuclear lamins, chromatin-associated factors or DNA (Boni et al., 2015; Powell and Burke, 1990; Ungricht et al., 2015a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Chromatin is the principal binding partner of INM proteins in all eukaryotes.
source: While the interaction of INM proteins with the nuclear lamina is restricted to lamin-expressing metazoan cells and certain protists, chromatin is the principal binding partner of INM proteins in all eukaryotes.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about INM protein interactions across eukaryotes.

claim: The lamin B receptor contains an N-terminal tudor domain for interaction with the epigenetically marked tail of histone H4.
source: The lamin B receptor (LBR), for example, contains an N-terminal tudor domain for interaction with the epigenetically marked tail of histone H4 as well as structurally less-defined regions for association with DNA and HP1 (Hirano et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hirano et al., 2012.

claim: Some INM proteins contain short bihelical motifs for chromatin interaction such as the LEM domain.
source: Some INM proteins contain short bihelical motifs for chromatin interaction such as the LEM (LAP2-emerin-MAN1) domain, which binds the chromatin factor BAF, or related motifs that bind DNA directly (Barton et al., 2015; Brachner and Foisner, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barton et al., 2015 and Brachner and Foisner, 2011.

claim: Many INM proteins might interact with DNA directly.
source: Biochemical experiments suggest that many INM proteins might even interact with DNA directly (Ulbert et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ulbert et al., 2006 and represents a speculative statement based on biochemical experiments.

claim: In cells undergoing open mitosis, the entire nuclear compartment is disintegrated by NE breakdown.
source: In cells undergoing open mitosis, the entire nuclear compartment is disintegrated by NE breakdown (NEBD), which liberates chromosomes from confinement by the nuclear membrane (Champion et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about open mitosis, supported by citation.

claim: During prophase, interactions between INM proteins, chromatin, and nuclear lamins are broken.
source: In the course of prophase, the multifaceted interactions between INM proteins, chromatin, and nuclear lamins are broken, allowing for the separation of membranes from chromatin and the partitioning of INM proteins into the mitotic ER network (Ellenberg et al., 1997; Yang et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ellenberg et al., 1997 and Yang et al., 1997.

claim: Failed removal of membranes from chromatin impairs mitotic chromatin organization, chromosome segregation and cytokinesis, and perturbs post-mitotic nuclear morphology.
source: Exploiting a synthetic membrane–chromatin tethering system, we recently demonstrated that failed removal of membranes from chromatin impairs mitotic chromatin organization, chromosome segregation and cytokinesis, and perturbs post-mitotic nuclear morphology (Champion et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Champion et al., 2019).

claim: Detachment of chromosomes from the NE is required for faithful chromosome segregation in yeasts with closed mitosis.
source: Notably, also in yeasts with closed mitosis, the detachment of chromosomes from the NE is required for faithful chromosome segregation (Titos et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Titos et al., 2014.

claim: Changes in posttranslational modifications of INM proteins and chromatin-associated factors induce membrane dissociation from chromatin during mitotic entry.
source: It is generally assumed that changes in posttranslational modifications of INM proteins and chromatin-associated factors, especially protein phosphorylation, induce membrane dissociation from chromatin during mitotic entry.
evidence: This represents a general assumption in the field based on established knowledge.

claim: Many mammalian INM proteins are phosphorylated in their nucleoplasmic domains by CDK1 or other abundant mitotic kinases during mitotic entry.
source: In strong support of this view, many mammalian INM proteins are phosphorylated in their nucleoplasmic domains by CDK1 or other abundant mitotic kinases during mitotic entry (Güttinger et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Güttinger et al., 2009.

claim: BAF is released from chromatin by mitotic phosphorylation.
source: Also chromatin-associated interaction partners of INM proteins such as BAF are released from chromatin by mitotic phosphorylation (Samwer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Samwer et al., 2017.

claim: LAP1 is an INM-localized activator of Torsins.
source: LAP1 is an INM-localized activator of Torsins; the only known AAA+ ATPases residing in the lumen of the ER and the continuous perinuclear space (Brown et al., 2014; Goodchild and Dauer, 2005; Laudermilch and Schlieker, 2016; Sosa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to Brown et al., 2014; Goodchild and Dauer, 2005; Laudermilch and Schlieker, 2016; Sosa et al., 2014.

claim: Torsins are the only known AAA+ ATPases residing in the lumen of the ER and the continuous perinuclear space.
source: LAP1 is an INM-localized activator of Torsins; the only known AAA+ ATPases residing in the lumen of the ER and the continuous perinuclear space (Brown et al., 2014; Goodchild and Dauer, 2005; Laudermilch and Schlieker, 2016; Sosa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents established knowledge about Torsin localization.

claim: Loss of Torsin functionality causes changes in NE morphology.
source: Although neither the precise biological role nor the substrates of Torsins are known, loss of Torsin functionality causes changes in NE morphology (Goodchild et al., 2005), pointing toward a role at the NE.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Goodchild et al., 2005.

claim: Mutations in TOR1A lead to early-onset dystonia (DYT1).
source: Mutations in TOR1A, the predominant Torsin isoform expressed in the brain (Jungwirth et al., 2010), lead to a severe movement disorder termed early-onset dystonia (DYT1) (Ozelius et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jungwirth et al., 2010 and Ozelius et al., 1997.

claim: Mutations in the LAP1 gene have been linked to primary dystonia, cardiomyopathy, cerebellar atrophy, and cancer.
source: Notably, also mutations in the LAP1 gene, which is ubiquitously expressed in the human body, have been linked to primary dystonia as well as to cardiomyopathy, cerebellar atrophy, and cancer (Dorboz et al., 2014; Fichtman et al., 2019; Kayman-Kurekci et al., 2014; Rebelo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dorboz et al., 2014; Fichtman et al., 2019; Kayman-Kurekci et al., 2014; Rebelo et al., 2015.

claim: Overexpression of LAP1B led to severe NE aberrations.
source: Remarkably, overexpression of LAP1B, the longest human isoform of LAP1, led to severe NE aberrations, while overexpression of other INM proteins did not cause similar defects (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1A comparing LAP1B to other INM proteins.

claim: Overexpression of other INM proteins (emerin, SUN1, SUN2, LAP2β, LEM2) did not cause NE aberrations similar to LAP1B.
source: Remarkably, overexpression of LAP1B, the longest human isoform of LAP1, led to severe NE aberrations, while overexpression of other INM proteins did not cause similar defects (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: LAP1-induced NE aberrations were observed in the vast majority of cells after 48 hr but not after 24 hr.
source: Interestingly, the LAP1-induced NE aberrations were observed in the vast majority of cells when analyzed after 48 hr, whereas most cells still displayed a normal nuclear morphology after 24 hr
evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of the phenotype shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Changes in NE morphology upon LAP1B expression were also evident in HCT116 and HepG2 cells.
source: Changes in NE morphology upon LAP1B expression were also evident in other cell types such as HCT116 or HepG2 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: LAP1B-GFP remained associated with chromatin throughout mitosis.
source: Strikingly, throughout mitosis, LAP1B-GFP remained associated with chromatin, and after NE reassembly, both daughter cells exhibited severe nuclear deformations.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1B and Video 1.

claim: LAP2β-GFP was faithfully released into the mitotic ER.
source: In contrast, LAP2β-GFP was faithfully released into the mitotic ER, and post-mitotic nuclei of LAP2β-GFP-expressing cells possessed a round unperturbed morphology (Figure 1B, Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1B and Video 2.

claim: The severity of NE aberrations increased with rising expression levels for both LAP1B-GFP and LAP1C-GFP.
source: The severity of the NE aberrations indeed increased with rising expression levels for both LAP1B-GFP and LAP1C-GFP (Figure 1D, E, F)
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1D, E, and F.

claim: NE aberrations were more pronounced for LAP1B than LAP1C when comparing cells with similar expression levels.
source: The severity of the NE aberrations indeed increased with rising expression levels for both LAP1B-GFP and LAP1C-GFP (Figure 1D, E, F); however, they were more pronounced for LAP1B when comparing cells with a similar expression level of both isoforms.
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 1D, E, and F.

claim: Both LAP1B-GFP and LAP1C-GFP were enriched at mitotic chromatin.
source: Both GFP-tagged LAP1 isoforms were enriched at mitotic chromatin; however, the enrichment of LAP1B-GFP was more prominent, indicating a stronger retention of the longer isoform on mitotic chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data of metaphase cells shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The enrichment of LAP1B-GFP at mitotic chromatin was more prominent than LAP1C-GFP.
source: Both GFP-tagged LAP1 isoforms were enriched at mitotic chromatin; however, the enrichment of LAP1B-GFP was more prominent, indicating a stronger retention of the longer isoform on mitotic chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Of the tested INM proteins, only LAP1B-GFP was strongly enriched at mitotic chromatin.
source: Analysis of metaphase cells revealed that of the tested INM proteins only LAP1B-GFP was strongly enriched at mitotic chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: LAP1B-GFP is a highly immobile INM protein.
source: Our FRAP experiments confirmed that LAP1B-GFP is a highly immobile INM protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: LAP1C-GFP was more mobile than LAP1B-GFP, showing a recovery curve similar to LAP2β-GFP.
source: In contrast, LAP1C-GFP was more mobile, showing a recovery curve similar to LAP2β-GFP.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Downregulation of lamin A/C and lamin B1, but not lamin B2, led to an increase in the diffusional mobility of LAP1B at the NE.
source: Downregulation of lamin A/C and lamin B1, but not of lamin B2, led to an increase in the diffusional mobility of LAP1B at the NE.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data after RNAi depletion shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Combined depletion of lamin A/C and lamin B1 had a stronger effect on LAP1B mobility than individual depletions.
source: The combined depletion of lamin A/C and lamin B1 had an even stronger effect, indicating that both A- and B-type lamins contribute to retention of LAP1B at the INM.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Both A- and B-type lamins contribute to retention of LAP1B at the INM.
source: The combined depletion of lamin A/C and lamin B1 had an even stronger effect, indicating that both A- and B-type lamins contribute to retention of LAP1B at the INM.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRAP experiments with lamin depletion shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: For LAP1C, only the loss of lamin A/C had a prominent effect on its mobility.
source: For LAP1C, only the loss of lamin A/C had a prominent effect on its mobility, suggesting that A-type lamins play a major role in retention of the shorter isoform at the INM.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: A-type lamins play a major role in retention of LAP1C at the INM.
source: For LAP1C, only the loss of lamin A/C had a prominent effect on its mobility, suggesting that A-type lamins play a major role in retention of the shorter isoform at the INM.
evidence: This is inferred from FRAP experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The extraluminal domain of LAP1B is predicted to be largely intrinsically disordered.
source: The extraluminal domain of LAP1B is predicted to be largely intrinsically disordered (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is based on computational prediction shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Two regions in LAP1B are sufficient for lamina association: an N-terminal fragment of 72 amino acids and a second region comprising residues 184–337.
source: By truncation analysis, we loosely delineated two regions in LAP1B that are sufficient for lamina association; an N-terminal fragment of 72 amino acids and a second region comprising residues 184–337 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C, D, E, F).
evidence: This is supported by truncation analysis and localization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The chromatin-binding region (CBR) of LAP1B maps to residues 98–136.
source: By testing further truncations, we mapped the chromatin-binding region (CBR) of LAP1B to residues 98–136 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by mapping experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The CBR (residues 98–136) is sufficient for chromatin interaction.
source: This protein fragment was very efficiently enriched on chromatin throughout mitosis (Figure 2C) and is sufficient for chromatin interaction.
evidence: This is supported by localization data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Deletion of the CBR from full-length, membrane-bound LAP1B-GFP abolished its association with chromatin during mitosis.
source: Importantly, deletion of the CBR from full-length, membrane-bound LAP1B-GFP abolished its association with chromatin during mitosis (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The CBR is sufficient to target a CBR-SPAG4-GFP fusion protein to the NE.
source: Consistent with our assumption that chromatin-binding contributes to the retention of LAP1B at the INM, the CBR was sufficient to target the CBR-SPAG4-GFP fusion protein to the NE (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by domain transfer experiments shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The purified recombinant CBR can interact with reconstituted nucleosomes and naked DNA.
source: Finally, we tested whether the CBR can interact with chromatin directly by performing electrophoretic mobility shifts assays (EMSAs), revealing that the purified recombinant CBR can interact with reconstituted nucleosomes and even naked DNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, D).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: Deletion of the CBR abolished the occurrence of NE aberrations caused by LAP1B expression.
source: Strikingly, deletion of the CBR abolished the occurrence of NE aberrations (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Mutations S108E and T124E affected NE localization of the LAP1(98–136)-SPAG4-GFP fusion protein during interphase.
source: With this approach, we identified two residues (S108 and T124) that if mutated to glutamate affected NE localization of the LAP1(98–136)-SPAG4-GFP fusion protein during interphase (Figure 2E)
evidence: This is supported by localization data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Mutations S108E and T124E abolished binding of LAP1(98–136)-SPAG4-GFP to chromatin in metaphase.
source: With this approach, we identified two residues (S108 and T124) that if mutated to glutamate affected NE localization of the LAP1(98–136)-SPAG4-GFP fusion protein during interphase (Figure 2E), abolished its binding to chromatin in metaphase (Figure 2E)
evidence: This is supported by localization data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Mutations S108E and T124E reduced the affinity of the CBR for DNA and mononucleosomes in vitro.
source: With this approach, we identified two residues (S108 and T124) that if mutated to glutamate affected NE localization of the LAP1(98–136)-SPAG4-GFP fusion protein during interphase (Figure 2E), abolished its binding to chromatin in metaphase (Figure 2E) and reduced its affinity for DNA and mononucleosomes in vitro (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, D).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: LAP1B(ΔCBR)-GFP and LAP1B-2E(S108E,T124E)-GFP exhibited higher mobility at the NE than wild-type LAP1B-GFP.
source: Comparison of the diffusional mobility of full-length LAP1B-GFP with LAP1B(ΔCBR)-GFP and LAP1B-2E(S108E,T124E)-GFP demonstrated that both mutant constructs exhibited a higher mobility at the NE, highlighting the contribution of the CBR and the identified residues to the retention of LAP1B at the INM (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: The CBR and residues S108 and T124 contribute to the retention of LAP1B at the INM.
source: Comparison of the diffusional mobility of full-length LAP1B-GFP with LAP1B(ΔCBR)-GFP and LAP1B-2E(S108E,T124E)-GFP demonstrated that both mutant constructs exhibited a higher mobility at the NE, highlighting the contribution of the CBR and the identified residues to the retention of LAP1B at the INM (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: This is inferred from FRAP data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: LAP1(1-359-2E)-GFP with S108E and T124E mutations showed abolished binding to mitotic chromatin and post-mitotic NE aberrations.
source: Importantly, when we introduced both mutations into the membrane-bound, nucleoplasmic domain of LAP1B in the construct LAP1(1-359-2E)-GFP, binding to mitotic chromatin and post-mitotic NE aberrations were fully abolished (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Chromatin-binding contributes to the retention of LAP1 at the NE.
source: Taken together, this data shows that chromatin-binding contributes to the retention of LAP1 at the NE
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data on CBR function and mobility.

claim: Residues S108 and T124 are essential for chromatin binding of LAP1B during mitosis.
source: Taken together, this data shows that chromatin-binding contributes to the retention of LAP1 at the NE and identifies two residues (S108 and T124) that are essential for chromatin binding of LAP1B during mitosis.
evidence: This is supported by the combined data from localization and EMSA experiments.

claim: There is a direct link between the CBR and post-mitotic NE aberrations.
source: Importantly, this establishes a direct link between the CBR and post-mitotic NE aberrations.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CBR deletion or mutation abolishes NE aberrations.

claim: Co-expression of Tor1A or Tor1B with LAP1B-GFP led to a striking decrease in NE aberrations.
source: Indeed, co-expression of either Torsin led to a striking decrease in NE aberrations (Figure 3A, B, C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3A, B, and C.

claim: Tor1B(E178Q)-HASt overexpression failed to rescue the NE aberrations caused by LAP1B-GFP.
source: In contrast to wild-type Torsins, Tor1B(E178Q)-HASt overexpression failed to rescue the NE aberrations caused by LAP1B-GFP, indicating that the enzymatic activity of Torsins is needed to prevent the LAP1B-induced phenotypes and not the LAP1B to Torsin ratio alone (Figure 3A, B, C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3A, B, and C.

claim: The enzymatic activity of Torsins is needed to prevent LAP1B-induced phenotypes.
source: In contrast to wild-type Torsins, Tor1B(E178Q)-HASt overexpression failed to rescue the NE aberrations caused by LAP1B-GFP, indicating that the enzymatic activity of Torsins is needed to prevent the LAP1B-induced phenotypes and not the LAP1B to Torsin ratio alone (Figure 3A, B, C).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of wild-type and ATPase-deficient Torsin effects shown in Figure 3.

claim: NE aberrations triggered by LAP1B(1-359)-GFP were not rescued by Tor1B-HASt overexpression.
source: As expected, NE aberrations triggered by expression of LAP1B(1-359)-GFP, which lacks the luminal domain required for Torsin activation, were not rescued by Tor1B-HASt overexpression (Figure 3A, B, C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A, B, and C.

claim: Tor1B co-expression did not ameliorate NE aberrations caused by LAP1B(R563G).
source: Similarly, Tor1B co-expression did not ameliorate NE aberrations caused by expression of LAP1B(R563G) (Figure 3E, F), a mutant inactivating the Arg-finger needed for stimulation of Torsin ATPase activity (Brown et al., 2014; Sosa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E and F, with citations to Brown et al., 2014 and Sosa et al., 2014.

claim: LAP1B(E482A) induced NE aberrations that were not prevented by Torsin co-expression.
source: Another non-functional LAP1B mutant, E482A, known to cause severe dystonia, cerebellar atrophy and cardiomyopathy (Dorboz et al., 2014), also induced NE aberrations, which were not prevented by Torsin co-expression.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E and F, with citation to Dorboz et al., 2014.

claim: Torsins can only act on LAP1 derivatives that are competent for activation of Torsin ATPase activity.
source: Thus, Torsins can only act on LAP1 derivatives that are competent for the activation of its ATPase activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that non-functional LAP1 mutants cannot be rescued by Torsin expression.

claim: Expression of LULL1 did not improve the NE shape of LAP1B-GFP expressing cells.
source: However, expression of LULL1 did not improve the NE shape of LAP1B-GFP expressing cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The correct LAP1B to Torsin ratio and functional interplay between LAP1B and Torsins ensure an unperturbed post-mitotic nuclear morphology.
source: Taken together, the correct LAP1B to Torsin ratio and the functional interplay between LAP1B and Torsins ensure an unperturbed post-mitotic nuclear morphology.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined rescue experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: LAP1B(R563G) and LAP1B(E482A) mutants were less mobile than wild-type LAP1B upon depletion of laminA/C and laminB1.
source: However, upon depletion of laminA/C and laminB1, it became apparent that both mutants were less mobile compared to the wild-type protein (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The dominant-negative Tor1B(E178Q) significantly reduced the mobility of LAP1B-GFP in laminA/C and B1-depleted cells.
source: The presence of the dominant-negative Torsin indeed significantly reduced the mobility of LAP1B-GFP in laminA/C and B1-depleted cells.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The LAP1-2E mutant was more mobile than wild-type LAP1B.
source: As expected, the LAP1-2E mutant was more mobile, and its mobility seemed less reduced by Tor1B(E178Q) expression.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Expression of LAP1B-GFP induced a two-fold increase in binucleated cells compared to the parental HeLa cell line.
source: Compared to the parental HeLa cell line, expression of LAP1B-GFP induced a two-fold increase in binucleated cells.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: LAP1B(1-359)-GFP and LAP1B(R563G)-GFP led to a twofold further rise in binucleated cells compared to LAP1B wild-type.
source: At a similar level, both LAP1B(1-359)-GFP and LAP1B(R563G)-GFP led to a twofold further rise in the number of binucleated cells compared to cells expressing LAP1B wild-type.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: LAP1B(E482A)-GFP caused an even higher number of binucleated cells than LAP1B(1-359)-GFP and LAP1B(R563G)-GFP.
source: This number was even higher for the disease-causing mutant LAP1B(E482A)-GFP.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: LAP1B(1-359-2E)-GFP did not cause binucleation, whereas LAP1B(1-359)-GFP caused binucleation in nearly 40% of cells.
source: Whereas LAP1B(1-359)-GFP caused binucleation in nearly 40% of cells under these conditions, LAP1B(1-359-2E)-GFP did not (Figure 5E, F), confirming that binucleation is caused by the LAP1B-chromatin interaction.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: Binucleation is caused by LAP1B-chromatin interaction.
source: Whereas LAP1B(1-359)-GFP caused binucleation in nearly 40% of cells under these conditions, LAP1B(1-359-2E)-GFP did not (Figure 5E, F), confirming that binucleation is caused by the LAP1B-chromatin interaction.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of wild-type and chromatin-binding-deficient mutants shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: RNAi-mediated depletion of lamin A/C and laminB1 in cells expressing LAP1B(1-359)-GFP did not reduce the number of binucleated cells.
source: As RNAi-mediated depletion of lamin A/C and laminB1 in cells expressing LAP1B(1-359)-GFP did not reduce the number of binucleated cells (Figure 5G, H), we conclude that the cell division defects are independent of nuclear lamins, and thus solely related to the aberrant binding of LAP1 to chromatin during mitosis.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: Cell division defects caused by LAP1B are independent of nuclear lamins and solely related to aberrant binding of LAP1 to chromatin during mitosis.
source: As RNAi-mediated depletion of lamin A/C and laminB1 in cells expressing LAP1B(1-359)-GFP did not reduce the number of binucleated cells (Figure 5G, H), we conclude that the cell division defects are independent of nuclear lamins, and thus solely related to the aberrant binding of LAP1 to chromatin during mitosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the lamin depletion experiments shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: Expression of Tor1B(E178Q)-GFP caused LAP1-positive patches to localize to (pro)-metaphase chromatin.
source: Strikingly, when we visualized endogenous LAP1 by immunofluorescence in cells expressing Tor1B(E178Q)-GFP, we observed LAP1-positive patches localizing to (pro)-metaphase chromatin, indicating an impaired release of LAP1 from chromatin during mitotic entry (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Cells expressing wild-type Tor1B-GFP showed GFP-positive membrane patches in the peripheral mitotic ER.
source: In comparison, cells expressing wild-type Tor1B-GFP showed GFP-positive membrane patches in the peripheral mitotic ER.
evidence: This is based on microscopy observations described in the text.

claim: Tor1B(E178Q)-GFP expression led to a twofold higher number of binucleated cells compared to cells expressing Tor1B-GFP wild-type.
source: Remarkably, Tor1B(E178Q)-GFP expression led to a twofold higher number of binucleated cells as compared to cells expressing Tor1B-GFP wild-type (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Tor1B(E178Q) expression caused a significant increase in chromosome segregation defects.
source: As binucleation is indicative for failed cytokinesis and commonly caused by chromosome segregation defects, we quantified DNA bridges and lagging chromosomes. This analysis revealed a significant increase in chromosome segregation defects (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The number of binucleated cells was significantly reduced in LAP1-depleted cells expressing Tor1B(E178Q)-GFP.
source: Importantly, the number of binucleated cells was significantly reduced in LAP1-depleted cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: LULL1 depletion did not reduce binucleation in Tor1B(E178Q)-GFP expressing cells.
source: For comparison, we also depleted the ER-resident Torsin-activator LULL1 in Tor1B(E178Q)-GFP expressing cells, but could not observe a reduction in binucleated cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, B, D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, B, and D.

claim: LULL1 depletion did not prevent the localization of LAP1 to mitotic chromatin upon Tor1B(E178Q) expression.
source: LULL1 depletion also did not prevent the localization of LAP1 to mitotic chromatin upon Tor1B(E178Q) expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C, D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: The dominant-negative Tor1B variant induces persistence of LAP1-positive membrane patches on (pro)-metaphase chromatin in a LAP1-dependent manner.
source: Taken together, the dominant-negative Tor1B variant induces the persistence of LAP1-positive membrane patches on (pro)-metaphase chromatin, chromosome segregation defects and binucleation in a LAP1-dependent manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing LAP1 localization and rescue by LAP1 depletion.

claim: Torsin function is important for mitotic fidelity by assuring normal LAP1 behavior during mitosis.
source: Collectively, our findings indicate that Torsin function is important for mitotic fidelity by assuring normal LAP1 behavior during mitosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the overall experimental findings showing that Torsin dysfunction leads to LAP1-dependent mitotic defects.

claim: LAP1 is tightly anchored at the INM of interphase cells by association with both chromatin and the nuclear lamina.
source: Our work uncovers that the abundant and ubiquitously expressed INM protein LAP1 is tightly anchored at the INM of interphase cells by association with both chromatin and the nuclear lamina.
evidence: This is supported by the combined data from FRAP experiments and mapping studies.

claim: LAP1 remains stuck on chromatin in mitosis if the stoichiometry of LAP1 to Torsins is unbalanced.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that LAP1 remains stuck on chromatin in mitosis if either the stoichiometry of LAP1 to Torsins is unbalanced or Torsin functionality is compromised.
evidence: This is supported by the overexpression experiments shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: LAP1 remains stuck on chromatin in mitosis if Torsin functionality is compromised.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that LAP1 remains stuck on chromatin in mitosis if either the stoichiometry of LAP1 to Torsins is unbalanced or Torsin functionality is compromised.
evidence: This is supported by the dominant-negative Torsin experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Torsins residing in the perinuclear space influence LAP1's ability to bind chromatin at the other side of the membrane.
source: Firstly, they indicate that Torsins, residing in the perinuclear space, influence LAP1's ability to bind chromatin at the other side of the membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental results showing trans-membrane effects.

claim: Failure in release of LAP1 from mitotic chromatin is associated with chromosome segregation defects, binucleation and postmitotic NE aberrations.
source: Secondly, reminiscent of some of the phenotypes that we have previously observed using a synthetic membrane-chromatin tether (Champion et al., 2019), the failure in release of LAP1 from mitotic chromatin is associated with chromosome segregation defects, binucleation and postmitotic NE aberrations.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 5 and 6, with citation to Champion et al., 2019.

claim: LAP1 might not merely be important for Torsin ATPase activation but itself subject to Torsin regulation across the INM.
source: Our experiments suggest that the interaction of Torsins with the C-terminal, luminal domain of LAP1 in the ER lumen influences the chromatin-binding activity of LAP1's nucleoplasmic domain on the other side of the membrane. This implies that LAP1 might not merely behave as an activator of Torsins, but could in turn itself be a downstream effector or 'substrate' influenced by the activity of the ATPases.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations showing bidirectional regulation.

claim: LAP1 might have a chromatin-associated function that is needed for proper development.
source: These severe defects are most likely caused by a lack of Torsin activation at the NE by lack of LAP1. However, it might also be worth considering whether LAP1 might have a chromatin-associated function that is needed for proper development.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential LAP1 functions.

claim: Primary dystonia caused by mutations of Tor1A or LAP1 seems to arise through dysfunction of post-mitotic neurons.
source: Given that primary dystonia caused by mutations of Tor1A or LAP1 seems to arise through a dysfunction of post-mitotic neurons, the function of Torsins is probably essential for the homeostasis of interphase cells.
evidence: This is based on knowledge about dystonia pathology.

claim: Mutation of LAP1's arginine finger was identified as a somatic mutation in melanoma and colon cancer.
source: Remarkably, mutation of LAP1's arginine finger was identified as a somatic mutation in melanoma (Krauthammer et al., 2012) and colon cancer (The Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Krauthammer et al., 2012 and The Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012.

claim: LAP1 is an activator of Tor1A and Tor1B.
source: LAP1 is an established activator of Torsin AAA+ ATPase family members, that is of Torsin1A (Tor1A) and Torsin1B (Tor1B) (Brown et al., 2014; Sosa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brown et al., 2014 and Sosa et al., 2014.

claim: Tor1B's in vitro ATPase activity can be more potently stimulated by LAP1 than that of Tor1A.
source: In the following, we continued our work with Tor1B, since it had been previously demonstrated that its in vitro ATPase activity can be more potently stimulated by LAP1 than that of Tor1A (Zhao et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2013.

claim: The luminal domains of LAP1 and LULL1 are structural mimics of the ATPase fold.
source: Furthermore, the luminal domains of LAP1 and LULL1 are structural mimics of the ATPase fold.
evidence: This represents established structural knowledge about LAP1 and LULL1.

claim: The luminal domains of LAP1 and LULL1 bind laterally to the ATPase domain of Torsins to activate ATP hydrolysis through their arginine finger.
source: These domains bind laterally to the ATPase domain of Torsins to activate ATP hydrolysis through their arginine finger (Brown et al., 2014; Sosa et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brown et al., 2014 and Sosa et al., 2014.

claim: Torsins have not been found to unfold the luminal domains of LAP1 and LULL1 in vitro.
source: Consistently, Torsins have not been found to unfold the luminal domains of LAP1 and LULL1 in vitro (Zhao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2013.

claim: Torsins can assemble into ATP-dependent, homo-oligomeric structures in vitro.
source: Indeed, Torsins can assemble into ATP-dependent, homo-oligomeric structures in vitro, adopting the configuration of a spiral or potentially a lock-washer (Chase et al., 2017; Demircioglu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chase et al., 2017 and Demircioglu et al., 2016.

claim: LAP1 and LULL1 are overstoichiometric to Torsins.
source: It remains to be seen which higher order configuration of Torsins exist in living cells, also in light of the view that LAP1 and LULL1 are overstoichiometric to Torsins (Itzhak et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Itzhak et al., 2016.

claim: LAP1 knockout mice exhibit perinatal lethality.
source: Notably, LAP1 is developmentally essential as LAP1 knockout mice exhibit perinatal lethality (Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2010.

claim: Loss of LAP1 expression in human patients has been associated with early onset multisystemic nuclear envelopathy.
source: Recently, loss of LAP1 expression in human patients caused by a mutation leading to an in-frame termination codon in LAP1 has been associated with an early onset multisystemic nuclear envelopathy manifesting in severe neurological and developmental deficiencies, resulting in early lethality of the patients (Fichtman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fichtman et al., 2019.

claim: The relative expression of LAP1B and LAP1C differs between tissues and changes during development.
source: Interestingly, the relative expression of LAP1B and LAP1C differs between tissues and changes during development (Santos et al., 2014; Shin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Santos et al., 2014 and Shin et al., 2014.

claim: Ser135 of LAP1 has been detected as mitotically phosphorylated in large scale phosphoproteomics.
source: While our own investigations of mitotic phosphorylation of these sites remained inconclusive, one of these residues, that is Ser135, has indeed been detected as mitotically phosphorylated in large scale phosphoproteomics (Dephoure et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dephoure et al., 2008.

claim: The nucleoplasmic domain of LAP1 is known to interact with protein phosphatase 1.
source: Interestingly, the nucleoplasmic domain of LAP1 is known to interact with protein phosphatase 1, the persistent binding of which could counteract the action of (mitotic) kinases (Santos et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Santos et al., 2013.
